messages.author: ac19819864ba3828
messages.subject: Operating on multiple columns
parts:
Hi,

I am a newcomer, therefore unable to figure it out. Requesting help ... 

Given the following: 

set.seed(5)
temp <- rnorm(500, mean=80, sd=12)
sales <- 2+temp*3

for(i in 1:length(sales)){
  if(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95) sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,25 )
  else sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,8 )
}


How can I replace the for loop, as in true spirit of R, with some "apply/plyr" function.


Cheers !

messages.author: 0dd6c9694b3c4809
messages.subject: Re: Operating on multiple columns
parts:
Looks fine to me: A nice explicit memorable, maintainable solution...
Maybe these loops are slightly better, but not everything needs applying, just because we have plyr :-)

for(i in seq_along(sales)) {
if(temp[i] < 75 | temp[i] > 95){ sd = 25 } else { sd = 8 }
sales[i] = sales[i] + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sd)
}

or
for(i in seq_along(sales)) {
x  = temp[i];
sd = ifelse(x < 75 | x > 95, 25, 8)
sales[i] = sales[i] + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = sd)
}

parts:
On Nov 24, 2013, at 7:00 AM, BHM wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I am a newcomer, therefore unable to figure it out. Requesting help ...
>
> Given the following:
>
> set.seed(5)
> temp <- rnorm(500, mean=80, sd=12)
> sales <- 2+temp*3
>
>
>
> for(i in 1:length(sales)){
>
>
> if(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95) sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,25 )
>
>
> else sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,8 )
> }
>
> How can I replace the for loop, as in true spirit of R, with some "apply/plyr" function.

sales <- sales + matrix(c( rnorm(500,0,8 ),
rnorm(500,0,25 )), ncol=2)[
cbind(1:500,1+())] )

For the "true spirit of R" you only need the "[" and cbind function to do some vectorized selection. The second column is coercing the "selection vector" from 500 logical 0/1's to indexing (1/2) of the first or second column of rnorm vectors in that two column matrix. I assure you it will be much faster than either the loop of an apply or plyr solution. The main efficiency is calling rnorm only twice.

Could also have used `ifelse` and I think this is both vectorized and easier to understand:

sales <- sales + ifelse( temp<75 | temp>95 , rnorm(500,0,25 ) , rnorm(500,0,8 ) )

Doing row oriented conditional operations will be quite slow.

--
David.

messages.subject: Re: Operating on multiple columns
parts:
Hi David,
ifelse on vectors is a big win! With length = 1e6, for loop = 10.3 seconds, vector ifelse = 0.68
Can chop that down further still with two vector updates and no ifelse (0.38 seconds).


set.seed(5)

temp  <- rnorm(1e6, mean=80, sd=12)

sales <- 2+temp*3


# ============

# = Method 1 =

# ============

ptm <- proc.time()

for(i in 1:length(sales)){

  if(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95) {

 sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,25 )

  } else {

 sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,8 )

  }

}

for(i in 1:length(sales)){

   if(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95) {

sales[i] <- sales[i]+2

   } else {

   sales[i] <- sales[i]+3

   }

}

proc.time() - ptm

 # user  system elapsed 

 #  4.763   0.034   4.767 


# ========================================================

# = Setting up an ifelse on each row is terrible idea... =

# ========================================================

ptm <- proc.time()

for(i in 1:length(sales)){

    sales[i] = sales[i] + ifelse(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95, rnorm(1,0,25 ), rnorm(1,0,8 ))

}

proc.time() - ptm

 #   user  system elapsed 

 # 20.863   0.128  20.901 


# ============================

# = Method 2:  vector ifelse =

# ============================

ptm <- proc.time()

sales <- sales + ifelse( temp<75 | temp>95 , rnorm(length(sales), 0, 25), rnorm(length(sales), 0, 8) ) 

proc.time() - ptm

 # user  system elapsed 

 # 0.643   0.033   0.680 


# ===========================

# = Method 3: Avoid ifelse  =

# ===========================

ptm <- proc.time()

sel = temp < 75 | temp > 95

sales[sel] <- sales[sel] + rnorm(sum(sel), 0, 25)

sales[!sel] <- sales[!sel] + rnorm(sum(!sel), 0, 8)

proc.time() - ptm

 # user  system elapsed 

 #  0.325   0.019   0.385

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Operating on multiple columns
parts:
This is the way you *should* do it, with ifelse():

df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length = 10), 0))
df.1$sales <- with(df.1, sales + ifelse(temp < 75 | temp > 95, 10, 100))
df.1

As others have mentioned, it is vectorized and faster than an if-else
construction. But to play along, if you're going to write a function
to pass to a **ply() function, it has to be compatible with the input
and output classes you define. For your toy example, I would rewrite
fn.1() as follows.

library(plyr)

# Notice that d is an object; e.g., an atomic vector or data.frame
fn.1 <- function(d)
{
if(d[["temp"]] < 75 | d[["temp"]] > 95)
{ d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 10}
else
{d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 100}
d
}

# These both yield the same output:

df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length = 10), 0))
ddply(df.1, .(), fn.1)
ddply(df.1, NULL, fn.1)

You get a warning with a column of NAs for the id column because
ddply() is expecting a quoted expression for its second argument. It
is designed for groupwise data processing, so when the groups aren't
there, you get unexpected output and warnings. Since the output object
is, apart from the NAs, the same as the input object, the function
never gets applied because of the input argument infelicities. (BTW,
out of curiosity, I'd be interested in the 'correct' way to do this,
if one exists.)

What you're trying to do is analogous to apply(df.1, 1, fn.1), so the
corresponding plyr function is adply() assuming you want data frame
output:

adply(df.1, 1, fn.1) # yields the expected output

In this case, adply() is expecting fn.1 to have an atomic vector as
input and a data frame (or something that can be coerced to a data
frame) as output. Since fn.1 is meant to operate on a single row and
both elements of a row happen to be numeric in this example, the input
to fn.1 could be either a numeric vector or a one-line data frame.

Dennis

On Tue, Nov 26, 2013 at 10:47 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
This is the way you *should* do it, with ifelse():

df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length = 10), 0))
df.1$sales <- with(df.1, sales + ifelse(temp < 75 | temp > 95, 10, 100))
df.1

As others have mentioned, it is vectorized and faster than an if-else
construction. But to play along, if you're going to write a function
to pass to a **ply() function, it has to be compatible with the input
and output classes you define. For your toy example, I would rewrite
fn.1() as follows.

library(plyr)

# Notice that d is an object; e.g., an atomic vector or data.frame
fn.1 <- function(d)
{
    if(d[["temp"]] < 75 | d[["temp"]] > 95)
       { d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 10}
    else
       {d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 100}
    d
}

# These both yield the same output:

df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length = 10), 0))
ddply(df.1, .(), fn.1)
ddply(df.1, NULL, fn.1)

You get a warning with a column of NAs for the id column because
ddply() is expecting a quoted expression for its second argument. It
is designed for groupwise data processing, so when the groups aren't
there, you get unexpected output and warnings. Since the output object
is, apart from the NAs, the same as the input object, the function
never gets applied because of the input argument infelicities. (BTW,
out of curiosity, I'd be interested in the 'correct' way to do this,
if one exists.)

What you're trying to do is analogous to apply(df.1, 1, fn.1), so the
corresponding plyr function is adply() assuming you want data frame
output:

adply(df.1, 1, fn.1)     # yields the expected output

In this case, adply() is expecting fn.1 to have an atomic vector as
input and a data frame (or something that can be coerced to a data
frame) as output. Since fn.1 is meant to operate on a single row and
both elements of a row happen to be numeric in this example, the input
to fn.1 could be either a numeric vector or a one-line data frame.

Dennis

parts:
Is this what you are looking for?

rm(list=ls())
library(plyr); library(microbenchmark); library(data.table)
fn.1 <- function(temp, sales) {
if(temp < 75 | temp > 95) val <- sales + 10 else val<- sales + 100
val
}
df.1 <- data.frame(id=1:10, sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120,
length = 10), 0))
df.2 <- ddply(df.1, .(id), mutate, sales.new=fn.1(temp, sales))
res.1 <- df.2$sales.new
res.2 <- with(df.1, sales + ifelse(temp < 75 | temp > 95, 10, 100))
all.equal(res.1, res.2)
microbenchmark(ddply(df.1, .(id), mutate, sales.new=fn.1(temp, sales)))
microbenchmark(with(df.1, sales + ifelse(temp < 75 | temp > 95, 10, 100)))
# On my system, ifelse is approximately 100 times faster than ddply
dt.1 <- data.table(df.1)
dt.1[temp < 75 | temp > 95, sales.new:= sales+10]
dt.1[temp > 75 & temp < 95, sales.new:= sales+100]
res.3 <- dt.1$sales.new
all.equal(res.1, res.3)
microbenchmark({dt.1[temp < 75 | temp > 95, sales.new:= sales+10]
dt.1[temp > 75 & temp < 95, sales.new:= sales+100]})
# On my system, ifelse is approximately 30-40 times faster than the
data.table route, and. data.table is faster than 2.5x than ddply

I don't know a better way to do that with data.table. I am pretty sure
that some one could do that more elegantly. And you can look at dplyr
for more benchmarking.

> # Interpreting the earlier comment "if is n't vectorized", I tried this:
>> fn.2 = colwise(fn.1)
>> fn.2(df.1)
>
> # With the result:
> Error in d[["temp"]] : subscript out of bounds
>
>
> Thanks again.
>
>
> Cheers !
>
>
> On Tue, Nov 26, 2013 at 10:47 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> This is the way you *should* do it, with ifelse():
>>
>> df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length =
>> 10), 0))
>> df.1$sales <- with(df.1, sales + ifelse(temp < 75 | temp > 95, 10, 100))
>> df.1
>>
>> As others have mentioned, it is vectorized and faster than an if-else
>> construction. But to play along, if you're going to write a function
>> to pass to a **ply() function, it has to be compatible with the input
>> and output classes you define. For your toy example, I would rewrite
>> fn.1() as follows.
>>
>> library(plyr)
>>
>> # Notice that d is an object; e.g., an atomic vector or data.frame
>> fn.1 <- function(d)
>> {
>> if(d[["temp"]] < 75 | d[["temp"]] > 95)
>> { d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 10}
>> else
>> {d[["sales"]] <- d[["sales"]] + 100}
>> d
>> }
>>
>> # These both yield the same output:
>>
>> df.1 <- data.frame(sales = seq(10), temp = round(seq(65, 120, length =
>> 10), 0))
>> ddply(df.1, .(), fn.1)
>> ddply(df.1, NULL, fn.1)
>>
>> You get a warning with a column of NAs for the id column because
>> ddply() is expecting a quoted expression for its second argument. It
>> is designed for groupwise data processing, so when the groups aren't
>> there, you get unexpected output and warnings. Since the output object
>> is, apart from the NAs, the same as the input object, the function
>> never gets applied because of the input argument infelicities. (BTW,
>> out of curiosity, I'd be interested in the 'correct' way to do this,
>> if one exists.)
>>
>> What you're trying to do is analogous to apply(df.1, 1, fn.1), so the
>> corresponding plyr function is adply() assuming you want data frame
>> output:
>>
>> adply(df.1, 1, fn.1) # yields the expected output
>>
>> In this case, adply() is expecting fn.1 to have an atomic vector as
>> input and a data frame (or something that can be coerced to a data
>> frame) as output. Since fn.1 is meant to operate on a single row and
>> both elements of a row happen to be numeric in this example, the input
>> to fn.1 could be either a numeric vector or a one-line data frame.
>>
>> Dennis
>>
>> On Tue, Nov 26, 2013 at 6:15 AM, BHM <ulh...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> > 2 <NA> 12
>> > 3 <NA> 13
>> > 4 <NA> 14
>> > 5 <NA> 15
>> > 6 <NA> 16
>> > 7 <NA> 17
>> > 8 <NA> 18
>> > 9 <NA> 19
>> > 10 <NA> 20
>> >
>> >
>> > # Output comes with a warning:
>> > ######################
>> > Warning message:
>> > In if (temp < 75 | temp > 95) { :
>> > the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
>> >
>> >
>> > Comment:
>> > For some reason - else clause never gets executed, though the temp data
>> > has
>> > a mix of values below, and above the if condition.
>> >
>> >
>> > Cheers !

>> > On Monday, November 25, 2013 8:51:02 AM UTC+5, David Winsemius wrote:

>> >> On Nov 24, 2013, at 1:01 PM, Timothy Bates wrote:

>> >> > Hi David,
>> >> > ifelse on vectors is a big win! With length = 1e6, for loop = 10.3
>> >> > seconds, vector ifelse = 0.68

>> >> >

>> >> > temp <- rnorm(1e6, mean=80, sd=12)
>> >> >
>> >> > sales <- 2+temp*3
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> > # ============
>> >> >
>> >> > # = Method 1 =

>> >> > sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,25 )
>> >> >
>> >> > } else {
>> >> >
>> >> > sales[i] <- sales[i]+rnorm(1,0,8 )
>> >> >
>> >> > }
>> >> >
>> >> > }
>> >> >
>> >> > proc.time() - ptm
>> >> >
>> >> > # user system elapsed
>> >> >
>> >> > # 10.135 0.273 10.381
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> > # =================================
>> >> >
>> >> > # = Around half the time in rnorm =
>> >> >
>> >> > # =================================
>> >> >
>> >> > ptm <- proc.time()
>> >> >
>> >> > for(i in 1:length(sales)){
>> >> >
>> >> > if(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95) {
>> >> >
>> >> > sales[i] <- sales[i]+2
>> >> >
>> >> > } else {
>> >> >
>> >> > sales[i] <- sales[i]+3
>> >> >
>> >> > }
>> >> >
>> >> > }
>> >> >
>> >> > proc.time() - ptm
>> >> >
>> >> > # user system elapsed
>> >> >
>> >> > # 4.763 0.034 4.767
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> > # ========================================================
>> >> >
>> >> > # = Setting up an ifelse on each row is terrible idea... =
>> >> >
>> >> > # ========================================================
>> >> >
>> >> > ptm <- proc.time()
>> >> > for(i in 1:length(sales)){
>> >> > sales[i] = sales[i] + ifelse(temp[i]<75 | temp[i]>95,
>> >> > rnorm(1,0,25
>> >> > ), rnorm(1,0,8 ))
>> >> > }

>> >> > # user system elapsed
>> >> > # 20.863 0.128 20.901
>> >> >
>> >> >

>> >> > # ============================
>> >> >

>> >> > 25), rnorm(length(sales), 0, 8) )
>> >> >
>> >> > proc.time() - ptm
>> >> > # user system elapsed

>> >> > # ===========================
